title: Notes from the Concert Hall
description: Ten texts about classical music and its instruments: how a piano sounds, a viola player's week, Bach's Leipzig, the conductor's gestures, a breathing organ, a quartet review, orchestra seating, a first cello lesson, a science evening on sound and the first night of The Rite of Spring.

lessons.title: Inside the Piano
lessons.summary: A short article explains how a piano makes its sound, how it was invented and why it needs care.
lessons.text:
Lift the lid of a grand piano and you will find something that looks less like a musical instrument than like a small factory. More than two hundred strings run from the front of the case to the back, stretched so tightly that together they pull with a force of about twenty tons. Under them lies a wide, thin sheet of wood, and in front of them sits a row of small wooden hammers covered in thick wool felt.

When a key is pressed, a chain of levers throws a hammer up against its strings. The hammer strikes and falls back at once, leaving the strings free to vibrate. A string alone, however, is too thin to move much air. Its energy passes through a wooden bridge into the sheet of wood, and the wood, with its large surface, moves the air in the same pattern. The strings decide the note; the wood gives it a voice.

The piano was invented in Florence circa 1700 by Bartolomeo Cristofori, a maker of keyboard instruments who worked for the Medici family. Circa is Latin for "around," and historians write circa 1700 because nobody knows the exact year. Unlike the harpsichord, the main keyboard of his day, Cristofori's instrument could play softly or loudly, depending on the player's touch.

The modern piano is the result of many iterations, and each iteration solved one problem while often creating another. Makers added more strings, then iron frames to hold their enormous pull, then a mechanism that let a note be repeated quickly. By the late nineteenth century, factories were producing upright pianos so inexpensive that ordinary families could buy one. For many households, an inexpensive upright was the first piece of furniture that was also a machine.

The felt on the hammers matters more than most listeners imagine. Hard felt gives a sound of great brightness; soft felt gives a darker, rounder tone. A knowledgeable technician can change the brightness of a single note by pricking the felt with fine needles. The same knowledgeable technician will notice when a hammer is defective, for example when its felt has worn flat and it buzzes instead of ringing. A defective hammer can often be repaired and kept usable for years; when it is no longer usable, it is replaced.

The greatest enemy of a piano is not a careless player but the weather. Wood swells in damp air and shrinks in dry air, so every fluctuation in humidity pulls the strings slightly out of tune. Technicians say that the optimum humidity for a piano lies between forty and fifty percent, and that steady conditions matter even more than the optimum number itself.

Anyone buying an old piano is therefore wise to bring a technician along. A purchaser who looks only at the polished case may take home a beautiful cabinet with a tired heart. A careful purchaser asks to see inside, where the hammers, the strings and the wood tell the true story.

Questions:
What happens to the hammer after it strikes the strings?
It falls back at once, leaving the strings free to vibrate.
Who invented the piano, and when?
Bartolomeo Cristofori invented it in Florence circa 1700.
How does the felt change the sound?
Hard felt gives brightness, while soft felt gives a darker, rounder tone.
Why does a fluctuation in humidity matter?
Because the wood swells or shrinks and pulls the strings out of tune.
What does a careful purchaser do?
A careful purchaser asks to see inside the piano.

lessons.title: A Week in the Viola Section
lessons.summary: A viola player in a regional orchestra describes an ordinary week of work, teaching, walks and one outdoor concert.
lessons.text:
I play the viola in a regional orchestra, and people who learn what I do usually ask one of two questions. The first is "What is a viola?" The second, from people who know, is "Have you heard any good viola jokes?"

The viola is a little larger than the violin and tuned lower, so its voice is darker and warmer. It rarely plays the tune; it lives in the middle of the harmony. As for the jokes, I have heard all of them, and viola players are known for being tolerant of them. You have to be tolerant when the whole orchestra thinks your instrument is funny.

My orchestra gives about thirty concerts a year. We are paid for each rehearsal and concert, and that is not enough to live on, so like most of my colleagues I build my livelihood from several pieces: the orchestra, fifteen private students, a church job and the occasional wedding. A livelihood made of pieces is less secure than a salary, but it is rarely boring.

Monday is my quiet day. I walk Pepper, my springer spaniel, along the river. A springer is a hunting dog with endless energy, and Pepper believes that every walk should last three hours.

Tuesday and Wednesday are rehearsals. I play in a gray hoodie and old jeans, as most of us do; black clothes are for concerts only. Our conductor once said that if he saw one more hoodie in the viola section, he would buy us all ties. Nobody believed him.

Playing for hours is hard on the body, so on Thursday mornings I go to a wellness class at the community center. It is taught by a gentle old man who grew up in India and spent many years in a monastery there. His students call him the swami, the title given in India to a respected religious teacher, and the swami accepts the name with a smile. I am not sure what wellness means exactly, but after his breathing exercises my neck stops hurting.

This Friday the orchestra played outdoors at the opening of a new park, where the governor gave a speech. Before we could reach the stage, we had to pass through a security checkpoint. At the checkpoint, a young guard opened my case, stared at my instrument and asked whether it was a small cello. During the concert, two bodyguards in dark suits stood behind the governor, completely still. I have never played for a more patient audience than those two bodyguards.

Afterward, a few of us went to a diner and ordered hamburgers. A hamburger after a concert is a tradition in our section: it is cheap, it is fast, and after three hours of playing we are always hungry.

On the weekend I taught and played at church, and on Monday, Pepper and I walked by the river again.

Questions:
Why are viola players tolerant of jokes?
Because the whole orchestra thinks their instrument is funny.
How does the narrator build her livelihood?
She builds it from the orchestra, private students, a church job and the occasional wedding.
What kind of dog is Pepper?
Pepper is a springer spaniel.
Who teaches the wellness class?
A gentle old man whom his students call the swami teaches it.
What did the guard at the checkpoint ask?
He asked whether her instrument was a small cello.

lessons.title: Bach's Week in Leipzig
lessons.summary: A historical account of how Johann Sebastian Bach worked in Leipzig, writing a new cantata almost every week.
lessons.text:
In 1723, Johann Sebastian Bach moved to Leipzig to become director of music at the St. Thomas School and the city's main churches. He was thirty-eight, and he stayed in Leipzig for the rest of his life.

The town council had not been eager to hire him; its first choice, Georg Philipp Telemann, had declined. The council was wary of Bach, who had no university degree and a reputation for being stubborn. They gave him the post on condition that he also teach Latin. Bach passed that duty to a deputy, whom he paid out of his own salary. It was a concession that suited both sides, and the first of many in a relationship that was never easy.

His main duty was the cantata, a work of twenty to thirty minutes for choir, singers and orchestra, performed during the Sunday service. The word comes from Italy and means "sung," and its plural is cantatas. In his first years in Leipzig, Bach wrote a new one almost every week. When scholars speak of his cantatas in the plural, they mean about two hundred works that survive; others have been lost.

The manuscripts suggest a likely pattern for such a week. Early in the week Bach composed, often at great speed. Next, the score was copied into separate parts for each performer, a task shared by his students, his older sons and his second wife, Anna Magdalena. Her handwriting came to look so much like his that experts have sometimes confused the two. After rehearsals, the cantata was performed on Sunday morning, in turns, at the churches of St. Thomas and St. Nicholas.

The boys of the school were his singers. For a talented boy, life there was a kind of apprenticeship in music: he sang, copied parts and watched a master at work. The apprenticeship had a hard side. The building was crowded, sanitation was poor by modern standards, and illness spread quickly. In 1730 Bach told the council in writing that his musicians were far from satisfactory. The council, in turn, found his own work less than satisfactory and reduced part of his income.

Money mattered to Bach, the father of a large family. Part of his income came from fees for funerals, and in a letter to an old friend he remarked that when the air in Leipzig was healthy, there were fewer funerals and his earnings fell. Still, it would be unfair to call him a mercenary. A mercenary works only for pay; Bach worked for pay and, as he wrote at the end of many scores, for the glory of God.

The pressure was immense, and the result was immensely rich. Bach's mastery grew week after week, under constant deadlines, in a crowded school, for a wary council and a congregation that expected new music every Sunday. Later composers admired that mastery immensely.

Questions:
Why was the council wary of Bach?
He had no university degree and a reputation for being stubborn.
What concession did Bach make about teaching Latin?
He passed the duty to a deputy, whom he paid himself.
Why have experts sometimes confused Anna Magdalena's handwriting with Bach's?
Because her handwriting came to look very much like his.
What was the hard side of the boys' apprenticeship?
The building was crowded, sanitation was poor and illness spread quickly.
Why is it unfair to call Bach a mercenary?
Because he worked for pay and also for the glory of God.

lessons.title: The Conductor's Silent Language
lessons.summary: An essay on how a conductor speaks to an orchestra without a sound, through the beat, the hands, the face and preparation.
lessons.text:
A conductor is the only musician on stage who makes no sound. Everything a conductor wants must be said in silence: with the baton, the left hand, the shoulders, the eyes and the breath. To the eighty people in front of the podium, it is a language, and like any language it can be spoken clearly or badly.

The basic grammar is the beat. The right hand, usually holding a baton, traces a pattern in the air: down for the first beat of the bar, then to the side and up. Every player watches the lowest point of that pattern, the moment when the baton seems to bounce. That is where the musicians' attention must converge. If eighty pairs of eyes converge on the same point at the same instant, the orchestra plays together. If they do not, the first chord sounds like a handful of gravel thrown at a window.

The left hand adds color. A palm turned down asks for quiet; a hand that rises slowly asks for more sound; a closed fist can mean a sudden stop. These signs are indicative rather than exact: they show a direction, not an amount. A good conductor knows when a gesture is ambiguous and replaces it with a clearer one, because an ambiguous gesture costs time in rehearsal, as the players stop and ask what was meant. Frequent questions are often indicative of unclear hands.

Much of the communication happens through the face. A raised eyebrow toward the trumpets says "not so loud." A small affirmative nod to a nervous flute player says "yes, now, I am with you." Players say that an affirmative look before a difficult solo can be worth more than an hour of advice.

Conductors differ greatly. Some are fiery, with large, sweeping gestures and a face that shows every feeling in the music. A fiery conductor can lift a tired orchestra, but too much movement can also mislead the players, who may not know which gestures matter and which are decoration. Others work with a certain detachment, moving little and letting the musicians listen to each other. Their detachment is a kind of trust. The danger at that end is a cavalier attitude toward details, the belief that the orchestra will simply manage. Players will forgive almost anything except a cavalier conductor who has not studied the score.

Behind the gestures lies preparation. Before the first rehearsal, a conductor spends weeks alone with the score, building a full comprehension of how the piece is made. That comprehension shows in the hands. Experienced players say they can tell within minutes whether a conductor truly knows the music, and their intuition is rarely wrong.

Gestures that mislead are, in the end, a form of noise. The art lies in saying exactly what is needed and nothing more.

Questions:
Where must the musicians' attention converge?
It must converge on the lowest point of the beat, where the baton seems to bounce.
Why does an ambiguous gesture cost time?
Because the players stop and ask what was meant.
What does an affirmative nod tell a nervous flute player?
It says "yes, now, I am with you."
What is the danger of a fiery conductor?
Too much movement can mislead the players.
How can experienced players tell whether a conductor knows the music?
Their intuition tells them, because the conductor's comprehension of the score shows in the hands.

lessons.title: How an Organ Breathes
lessons.summary: An organ builder shows a visitor how a church organ makes its sound, a week before the restored instrument is played again.
lessons.text:
On a cold morning in late autumn, the organ builder Martin Hale climbed a narrow ladder behind the organ of a small stone church, and I followed. The church had saved for nine years to restore its instrument, and the inauguration of the restored organ was planned for the following Sunday.

"People think of the organ as a keyboard instrument," Hale said. "It is really a wind instrument. It breathes."

In the past, the air was supplied by men who pumped large leather bags with their feet or hands. Today an electric fan fills a wooden box whose lid, pressed down by heavy weights, keeps the pressure steady. From there the air travels to the pipes. When the organist presses a key, a small door opens under a pipe, and the air rushes in.

Each pipe plays only one note, so a large organ needs thousands of them, from tubes taller than a house to tubes shorter than a pencil. They are grouped in families, and each family has its own color: soft like a flute, bright like a trumpet, or rich like a string section. The largest pipes give the deep, majestic sound that most people think of when they hear the word organ.

Many of the pipes are made of an alloy of tin and lead. Hale pointed to a box of old pipes and told me to wear gloves. Lead is poisonous, he explained, and workers who cut and melt it must protect themselves from its poisonous dust. The exact mixture of metals used to be a matter of secrecy, passed from master to apprentice inside each workshop. Today that secrecy is mostly gone.

An organ in an old church lives in peril. Damp air makes wood swell and metal decay, but the greatest peril of all is fire, since an organ is a large wooden structure full of dry air.

The keyboards combine old and new. Under the bench, below keys that look as they did in 1890, sits a small onboard computer. The onboard system lets the organist store combinations of sounds and recall them with one button. Hale spent weeks adjusting each pipe to optimize the sound for this particular building. "You cannot optimize an organ in the workshop," he said. "The room is part of the instrument."

In a stone church, a chord does not stop when the organist lifts her hands. It lingers in the air for two or three seconds, and the sound that lingers is a large part of what people mean when they call an organ majestic.

On the way out, I noticed that the path to the church door was lined with veronica, a garden plant with tall spikes of small blue flowers. Hale told me that members of the church had planted the veronica for the inauguration. On Sunday, he said, the doors would be open, and anyone walking past the flowers would hear the old organ breathe again.

Questions:
Why does the organ builder say that the organ breathes?
Because it is really a wind instrument, and air must flow through its pipes.
Why must workers be careful with old pipes?
Because the pipes contain lead, which is poisonous.
What does the onboard computer do?
It lets the organist store combinations of sounds and recall them with one button.
Why can an organ builder not optimize an organ in the workshop?
Because the room is part of the instrument.

lessons.title: Review: The Alder Quartet
lessons.summary: A critic reviews a concert by a young string quartet that played Haydn, Puccini and Shostakovich in a small hall.
lessons.text:
It is not often that a concert in an old farm building leaves a critic searching for words, but on Thursday evening the Alder Quartet did exactly that. Their playing has the energy of a youthful group and the discipline of a much older one, and the combination was hard to resist.

They began with a quartet by Haydn from 1781, known as "The Joke." Haydn was a witty composer, and this is one of his most famous endings: the last movement seems to finish several times, with long silences between the phrases, until the audience no longer knows when to applaud. The Alder players understood that the joke works only if it is played completely straight. They waited through each silence without a smile, and the audience laughed at exactly the right moments. It was witty playing of the best kind, the kind that trusts the music.

Next came a short piece that many groups treat as filler: Crisantemi, a six-minute song of mourning for strings that Puccini wrote in 1890. Audiences often use such filler as a chance to read their programs. Not this time. The first violin, Clara Voss, played its long melody with no trace of the diva about her. A diva would have made the piece about herself; Voss made it about the music, and the hall went very quiet.

After the break came the Eighth Quartet of Shostakovich, written in 1960. Shostakovich had been publicly attacked by the Soviet government in 1936 and again in 1948. Although he was never arrested, he lived for years in fear, as he watched the state persecute many of his friends. The quartet, written in three days, quotes many of his earlier works, like a musical autobiography. It is a heartbreaking piece, and the Alder Quartet did not soften it. The slow last movement, which seems to fade into silence, was simply heartbreaking.

The cello player, Tomas Brandt, is something of a maverick. He plays without the metal spike that holds most cellos off the floor, gripping the instrument between his knees as players did in Haydn's time, and he sometimes chooses tempos that surprise his colleagues.

As an encore they played the fast finale of a Beethoven quartet, and the evening ended in a mood that felt almost victorious, as if the musicians and the audience had come through something difficult together. The victorious last chords brought the audience to its feet.

I will admit that I have become a cheerleader for this group. Critics are not supposed to be cheerleaders, but it is hard to stay neutral when a youthful ensemble plays with such honesty. The hall was half empty, which is shameful in a town that claims to love music. It would be shameful if a group of this quality had to leave us to find full houses elsewhere.

Questions:
Why did the audience laugh at the right moments during the Haydn?
Because the players waited through each silence without a smile.
How do audiences often treat a short filler piece?
They use it as a chance to read their programs.
Why did Shostakovich live in fear?
He had been publicly attacked, and he watched the state persecute many of his friends.
Why is the cello player called a maverick?
He plays without the metal spike and sometimes chooses surprising tempos.
What does the critic think is shameful?
The critic thinks it is shameful that the hall was half empty in a town that claims to love music.

lessons.title: Who Sits Where
lessons.summary: A short history of how the seats of a symphony orchestra came to be arranged as they are today.
lessons.text:
Walk into almost any concert hall today and you will see the same arrangement: the violins on the conductor's left, the lower strings in the middle and on the right, the wind players in rows in the center, and the brass and drums at the back. It looks so natural that listeners often assume, incorrectly, that it is as old as the symphony itself. In fact, it is only about a hundred years old.

In the age of Haydn and Mozart there was no conductor in the modern sense. The orchestra was usually led from the keyboard by the composer, or by the first violin. Old paintings of concerts often show the players as small, unnamed figures crowded around a keyboard.

Concerts were also a matter of entrepreneurship. In London, the violin player Johann Peter Salomon rented halls, hired musicians and sold tickets, and in 1791 he brought Haydn from Vienna for a famous series of concerts. Salomon's entrepreneurship gave Haydn a large new public.

The leader of today's violins, who walks on stage last and shakes the conductor's hand, is a hangover from those days. The custom no longer has any practical purpose, but like many a hangover from the past, it survives because people like it.

Through the nineteenth century, orchestras commonly divided the violins. The first violins sat on the conductor's left and the second violins on the right, facing them across the stage. Composers such as Beethoven, Brahms and Tchaikovsky wrote with this in mind, sometimes passing a melody from one side to the other, so that the music seemed to travel through the air.

In the twentieth century, Leopold Stokowski of the Philadelphia Orchestra tried almost every arrangement, even the winds in front of the strings. Some players complained that he behaved like an anarchist, tearing down a tradition that had worked for a century. But Stokowski was no anarchist. His aim was a richer, more unified sound, especially for recordings and radio. The layout he favored placed all the violins together on the left. It is sometimes said, perhaps incorrectly, that he invented it; what is certain is that he did more than anyone to spread it.

Many second violin players regarded the move as a downgrade. Seated behind the first violins, with their instruments pointing away from the audience, they felt that they could no longer be heard. For them it was a downgrade in sound as well as in status.

After the Second World War, the new layout spread across Europe and Asia. Its success was an early form of globalization: as orchestras toured, recorded and shared conductors, one arrangement became the standard. Critics of this globalization argue that it has made orchestras sound more alike.

Today, some conductors are moving the second violins back to the right, where Beethoven and Brahms expected them. The debate shows that the orchestra is still a living thing.

Questions:
How do old paintings of concerts show the players?
They show them as small, unnamed figures crowded around a keyboard.
What did Johann Peter Salomon do?
He organized concerts and brought Haydn to London.
Why is the handshake with the conductor called a hangover?
Because it survives from an earlier time, although it has no practical purpose.
Why did some players say that Stokowski behaved like an anarchist?
They felt he was tearing down a tradition that had worked for a century.
Why was the new layout a downgrade for second violin players?
They felt that they could no longer be heard.

lessons.title: Nora's First Cello Lesson
lessons.summary: A seven-year-old girl drives through a snowstorm to her first cello lesson and plays her first real note.
lessons.text:
Nora was seven when she decided that she wanted to play the cello. She had seen one at a school concert and had come home talking about "the big violin that you hug." Her grandmother, who loved books, found the instrument in an old encyclopedia and read the entry to her. The encyclopedia said that the cello had four strings and was played with a bow.

The encyclopedia also taught Nora something about pronunciation. She had been saying the word as if it began like "sell." Her grandmother explained that the word came from Italy, and that its pronunciation began with the same sound as "chair."

Her first lesson was on a Saturday in January. That morning a blizzard came down from the north, and her father wondered whether they should stay home. Nora would not hear of it. They drove slowly through the blizzard and arrived ten minutes late at the small yellow house of Mrs. Lind, the teacher.

Mrs. Lind's house smelled of rosemary. She grew it in pots by every window and said that rosemary liked the cold light of winter as much as she did. She gave Nora's father a cup of hot apple cider and sent him to the kitchen to wait. "Parents may listen," she said with a smile, "but they may not snoop." Her father went willingly, with his cider and a newspaper, although Nora suspected that he would snoop anyway from behind the door.

The cello Nora would rent was a small one, made for children. Mrs. Lind showed her how to sit at the front of the chair, how to let the cello lean against her chest, and how to hold the bow with a soft, round hand. "Hold the bow the way you would hold a baby bird," she said.

Nora was nervous. Her first sound was a terrible scratching noise, and she turned red. Mrs. Lind made a goofy face and a goofy noise of her own on her big cello, so that they both laughed. "Everyone in the world started with that sound," she said.

Then she told Nora to stay calm and pull the bow slowly, "cool as a cucumber." Nora did not know what a cucumber had to do with music, but she understood that it meant calm. She breathed out and pulled the bow slowly across the lowest string. This time, the cello gave a deep, warm note that she could feel in her chest. She played the note again and again, cool as a cucumber, until it was steady.

At the end of the lesson, Mrs. Lind gave her a small souvenir: a tiny block of the hard, sticky material that players rub on their bows, wrapped in paper. Nora held the souvenir in her hand all the way home. The blizzard had stopped, and the fields were white and silent.

That evening, Nora willingly practiced for twenty minutes without being asked.

Questions:
What did the encyclopedia tell Nora?
It said that the cello had four strings and was played with a bow.
What did Nora learn about the pronunciation of the word?
She learned that it began with the same sound as "chair."
What did Mrs. Lind say about parents?
She said that parents may listen, but they may not snoop.
Why did Mrs. Lind make a goofy face?
She made it so that Nora would laugh after her first terrible sound.

lessons.title: Seeing Sound
lessons.summary: At a college science evening, a physicist and a bass player show an audience what sound is and how it travels.
lessons.text:
Every spring, the physics department of a small college in Ohio holds an evening called "Seeing Sound." This year it was led by Dr. Amina Ross, a physicist, and her friend Paul, who plays the double bass in the local orchestra. More than a hundred people came, many of them children.

In her laboratory, Dr. Ross works with neutrons and protons, the tiny particles in the center of every atom. "Sound is not made of neutrons or protons or anything else that flies through the air," she said. "Sound is a wave of pressure. The air itself only moves back and forth a little; what travels across the room is the pattern."

She compared sound to a tsunami. In the open ocean, a tsunami may be less than a meter high, and a ship can pass over it without noticing. The water mostly rises and falls in place, while the energy of the tsunami races across the ocean almost as fast as a jet plane.

Then Paul struck a large brass gong that stood on the stage, and its deep note filled the hall. Children in the front row touched the edge of the gong gently and felt it shaking under their fingers. "That shaking," Dr. Ross said, "is the beginning of every sound you have ever heard."

The most popular part of the evening was a long metal pipe with a row of small holes along the top. The pipe was filled with gas, and a small flame burned at each hole. Dr. Ross explained that the flames came from combustion, the chemical reaction of the gas with the oxygen in the air, and that each flame's height depended on the gas pressure beneath it. When Paul played a long, low note, a speaker at one end sent the sound into the pipe, and the row of flames formed a wave, tall in some places and short in others. The audience could see the shape of the note.

At one point the flames began to jump strangely, and a faint smell of gas reached the first rows. Dr. Ross quietly decided to abort the demonstration. She turned off the gas and asked Paul to disconnect the speaker. "When you work with combustion," she told the audience, "you disconnect, you abort, and you ask questions later." After a loose connection was fixed, the demonstration began again.

For the last part, Dr. Ross asked a girl named Rosa to sing one long note while changing the vowel: first "ah," then "ee," then "oo." A computer showed the sound on a large screen as colored bands. Each vowel made a different pattern, even though the note stayed the same. "When you change the vowel, you change the shape of your mouth," Dr. Ross said, "and the sound changes with it." After that, half the children in the hall wanted to sing to the screen.

Questions:
What does Dr. Ross study in her laboratory?
She works with neutrons and protons.
Why did she compare sound to a tsunami?
Because in both cases the water or air stays in place while the energy travels.
What did the children feel when they touched the gong?
They felt it shaking under their fingers.
Why did Dr. Ross abort the demonstration?
Because the flames began to jump strangely and there was a faint smell of gas.
What happened on the screen when Rosa changed the vowel?
Each vowel made a different pattern, even though the note stayed the same.

lessons.title: The Night of The Rite of Spring
lessons.summary: An account of the famous first performance of Stravinsky's ballet in Paris in 1913, and of how it was received a year later.
lessons.text:
On the evening of 29 May 1913, a fashionable audience gathered at a new theater in Paris for the first performance of a ballet called The Rite of Spring. The music was by Igor Stravinsky, a thirty-year-old composer from Russia. The dances were by Vaslav Nijinsky, the most celebrated dancer of his day. The company was the Ballets Russes, directed by Sergei Diaghilev, and since 1909 Paris had been in the grip of a craze for everything it produced. The audience expected something beautiful.

What they heard first was a single bassoon, a low wooden wind instrument, playing a melody so high that it hardly sounded like a bassoon at all. Pushed to the top of its range, the instrument produces a thin, tight tone, and some listeners described it as strangled. To ears used to smooth, singing melodies, that strangled sound was a shock. Laughter began within minutes.

When the curtain rose, the dancers did not leap lightly, as ballet dancers were expected to do. They stamped, turned their toes in and moved like people under a spell. The laughter turned to shouting, and supporters of the new work shouted back. Soon the din in the hall was so great that the dancers could no longer hear the orchestra. Nijinsky stood on a chair at the side of the stage and shouted the counts to them, while the conductor, Pierre Monteux, kept the orchestra playing through the din.

How bad was it? Here the accounts disagree, and later legends can mislead us. Some writers describe fights in the aisles. Some say that the police were called and that a number of people were ejected from the theater; others do not mention anyone being ejected at all. Several witnesses wrote down their memories decades later, when the story had already grown.

Historians also ask whether the work really did incite the disorder. Some believe that groups in the audience came ready to protest, so that the music did not incite the noise but only provided the occasion. Others think that the strange music and strange dancing were enough to anger a crowd that had come expecting pleasure.

For Stravinsky, the evening could have been a humiliation. He left his seat and spent the rest of the performance behind the stage, angry and upset. Whatever the truth, news of the scandal spread like wildfire. Within days, the story had moved like wildfire through the newspapers of Europe.

The humiliation, if it was one, did not last. In April 1914, Monteux conducted the music without the dancers at a concert in Paris. This time the audience cheered, and Stravinsky was carried out of the hall on the shoulders of his supporters. Today The Rite of Spring is one of the most frequently performed works of the twentieth century.

Questions:
What had Paris been in the grip of since 1909?
Paris had been in the grip of a craze for everything the Ballets Russes produced.
Why did some listeners describe the opening as strangled?
Because the bassoon, pushed to the top of its range, produced a thin, tight tone.
How did Nijinsky help the dancers through the din?
He stood on a chair and shouted the counts to them.
Do historians agree that the music incited the disorder?
No. Some believe that groups came ready to protest, while others think the music and dancing were enough.
What happened at the concert in April 1914?
The audience cheered, and Stravinsky was carried out on the shoulders of his supporters.
